Banco BPM took 89.959% in April 2025 at EUR 7.00 and stopped one-twentieth of a percentage point short of the threshold that would have bought you out. interrogator_dossier:
# Anima Holding S.p.A. (ANIM.MI) — a deep dive on management and the setup

**Date of review:** 27 July 2026 · **Price used:** €6.94 (Euronext Milan close, 27 July 2026, −1.8% on the day) · **Market value:** about €2.26 billion on roughly 325 million shares

**A note on sources before anything else.** Anima does not publish English-language quarterly earnings-call transcripts, and our data vendor holds none for this listing. There is therefore no multi-quarter transcript series to interrogate, and I will not invent one. What follows is built from what can actually be sourced: the company's own quarterly result releases (most recently the first quarter of 2026, published 4 May 2026), its monthly flow disclosures, the Italian financial press, the Borsa Italiana corporate calendar, and the hard financials in our screener and from the data vendor as of today. Where a management quote appears, it is a translation of the Italian press release as reported by Teleborsa, and it is labelled as such. Where I could not source something, I say so.

---

## 1. Narrative arc

Anima is Italy's largest independent asset manager: it runs mutual funds, institutional mandates and insurance money, with about €203 billion of client assets at the end of March 2026. Almost all of that money reaches Anima through other people's branches — the bank networks of Banco BPM, Monte dei Paschi di Siena, Poste Italiane and Crédit Agricole Italia. That single fact explains both the story management tells and the story the market is actually pricing.

Over the past five years the arc has moved through three phases.

**Phase one (2021–2023) — the fee reset.** Gross commission income fell from €1.23 billion in 2021 to €1.02 billion in both 2022 and 2023, and net income halved from €239 million to €121 million in 2022. This was the bond-market shock working through a book that is unusually heavy in fixed income and insurance-linked products, plus the disappearance of performance fees (the extra fee an asset manager earns only when funds beat a benchmark). Management's language in that period was defensive and cost-focused.

**Phase two (2024–2025) — recovery plus acquisition.** Revenue recovered to €1.32 billion in 2024 and €1.43 billion in 2025, and net income to €228 million and then €266 million. Two things drove it: performance fees came back, and Anima bought its way into new areas — most visibly Castello SGR, a real-estate and alternatives manager, and a broader push beyond plain mutual funds. The narrative shifted from "protect the margin" to "diversify the revenue mix."

**Phase three (from November 2024 to now) — the story stops being about Anima.** On 6 November 2024 Banco BPM launched a takeover for the shares of Anima it did not already own, at €6.20, later raised to €7.00, explicitly aiming to take Anima private. The offer closed in April 2025 with Banco BPM at 89.959% — agonisingly short of the 90% that would have forced a buy-out of the rest and a delisting. Anima has therefore been left as a listed remnant: roughly a tenth of the company still floats, and the other nine-tenths sits with a parent that has said in writing it would rather not have a listing at all.

Since then the operating narrative has become almost secondary. What moves this share is the Italian banking reshuffle: Intesa Sanpaolo's roughly €30.6 billion exchange offer for Monte dei Paschi launched on about 8 June 2026, Monte dei Paschi's board rejecting it as too cheap on 16 July 2026, and the counter-plan for Monte dei Paschi to merge with Banco BPM instead — reported through late July as targeted for early August, with Crédit Agricole (Banco BPM's largest shareholder) publicly cool on it as of 22 July.

---

## 2. Claims versus financials

Management's core claims are that revenue is growing, costs are falling, the mix is diversifying, and the underlying profit is rising even when the headline profit is not. Here is how each holds up.

| Management claim | The evidence | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| Revenue is growing | First-quarter 2026 net revenue €140.6 million, up 5% year on year; net management fees €92.1 million, also up 5% | Holds. Modest, but real and fee-driven rather than one-off |
| Costs are under control | First-quarter 2026 operating costs €39.5 million, down 1%; cost-to-income ratio 35.5% | Holds, and this is genuinely good. A cost-to-income ratio in the mid-thirties is top-quartile for a European asset manager |
| Profit is rising | Reported net income fell 14% to €61.4 million; the "normalised" figure rose 13% to €69.9 million | Holds, but only with the footnote. The 14% fall is explained by €31.8 million of one-off distributor revenue booked in the first quarter of 2025. The comparison base, not the business, moved |
| Client assets are growing | €203.3 billion at March 2026 versus €202.1 billion a year earlier (+1%), but down from €212 billion at December 2025 | Weaker than the story. Net flows in the first quarter were minus €5.8 billion, of which €5.7 billion was the previously-flagged exit of the Etica SGR mandate. Strip that out and flows were roughly flat, not growing |
| Diversification is working | Castello SGR taken to 100% on 29 June 2026, buying Oaktree's remaining 20% for €19 million | Holds directionally, but the scale is small. €19 million for a fifth of Castello implies about €95 million for all of it — roughly 4% of Anima's market value |

Two divergences deserve emphasis.

**The revenue line is not what it looks like.** The €1.47 billion of trailing twelve-month "revenue" in the vendor data is *gross* commission income. Roughly 63% of it is paid straight back out to the banks that distribute the funds. Anima's own reported net revenue runs at about €560 million a year. Anyone anchoring on the €1.47 billion figure — or on a price-to-sales ratio of 1.5 times — is measuring the wrong thing.

**Roughly one fifth of net revenue is performance fees, and those are a market bet.** Performance fees were €29.3 million of the €140.6 million first-quarter net revenue. That slug is genuinely earned, but it appears when markets rise and vanishes when they do not. It disappeared almost entirely in 2022. Any valuation that capitalises it at the same multiple as management fees is overpaying.

Underneath, the returns are respectable and stable: return on equity of 14.3% and return on invested capital of 8.4% on the trailing twelve months, free cash flow of about €250 million against a market value of €2.26 billion (an 11% free-cash-flow yield), and a Piotroski score of 7 out of 9. The balance sheet carries €869 million of cash and short-term investments against €840 million of debt — essentially flat, about €30 million of net cash, or nine cents a share. Anima's own wider measure of its financial position, which also counts longer-dated financial investments, was €558.3 million at the end of March. The gap between those two numbers is the roughly €500 million of investment assets on the books, part of which is seed capital and regulatory capital that is not freely available to shareholders.

One number in the screener's model stack should be discarded outright: a Graham-style margin of safety of +80%. That method leans on book value, and Anima's €5.77 per share of book value is €4.63 per share of goodwill and intangibles — over half of total assets. On tangible book the figure is €1.14 a share. A book-value method applied to an acquisitive asset manager is measuring purchase accounting, not value.

---

## 3. Tone and confidence trajectory

**Stable.** With no call transcripts to trace, the read has to come from the written releases, and those have been consistent rather than escalating. Chief executive Saverio Perissinotto's comment alongside the first-quarter 2026 results (as translated from the Italian release by Teleborsa, 4 May 2026) was that the quarter closed with solid earnings and constructive expectations for the year "despite evident external headwinds," crediting channel diversification and operational efficiency.

That is measured language, and notably it concedes the headwind rather than talking past it. There is no shift into defensive cost-cutting vocabulary — costs are already low and falling — but neither is there the offensive, investment-led language of a company with a growth runway it wants to fund. The tone is that of a mature, well-run utility-like business under an owner that has already decided its future.

---

## 4. Guidance credibility

**Medium-to-high.** Anima does not give the kind of granular forward guidance that can be scored line by line, but three proxies point the same way. First, the delivery record: our screener shows the company beating consensus in six of the last seven quarters (86%). Second, the Etica SGR mandate loss — €5.7 billion of outflow — was pre-announced rather than sprung on the market, which is the behaviour of a management team that does not manage the news. Third, the reported-versus-normalised gap in the first quarter was clearly bridged to a specific, identifiable prior-year item (€31.8 million of distributor revenue in the base quarter) rather than hidden behind an adjective.

Against that, the consensus now looks for forward earnings per share to *fall* about 2%. Management has not publicly contested that, which suggests either quiet agreement or an absence of the promotional instinct. On this evidence I read it as the latter.

There is one credibility issue in the file, and it belongs to the parent rather than to Anima. On 23 June 2026 Consob, the Italian market regulator, sanctioned Banco BPM for the delay in disclosing that the European Central Bank would not allow the favourable "Danish Compromise" capital treatment to be applied to its Anima acquisition. That is a disclosure failure by the shareholder that controls 90% of this company, on a matter that goes directly to how expensive it is for that shareholder to keep owning Anima. Minority holders should file it.

---

## 5. Analyst pressure points

Without call transcripts I cannot list questions management deflected. What I can identify are the questions the published materials do not answer, and which any owner of the minority shares needs answered:

- **What happens to the Monte dei Paschi distribution relationship?** Milano Finanza described Monte dei Paschi (11 June 2026) as Anima's principal distributor, and named protecting that alliance as a strategic consideration in how Banco BPM responds to Intesa Sanpaolo. If Intesa Sanpaolo wins Monte dei Paschi, Intesa owns its own large asset manager and has every commercial reason to migrate that money to it over time. Neither Anima nor Banco BPM has publicly quantified what is at stake.
- **What does the parent intend to do with the remaining 10%?** Banco BPM reserved the right to consider future initiatives on the residual stake after April 2025. Fifteen months later there has been no offer, no market buying disclosed to take it past 90%, and no timetable.
- **How much of the €500 million of financial investments is actually surplus?** The company reports a net financial position of €558.3 million but the strict cash-minus-debt figure is €30 million. The bridge is not broken out for outside investors.
- **Where does organic growth come from?** June 2026 managed net inflows, excluding class-I insurance products, were €202 million. On a €203 billion book that is a rounding error. The growth in the profit-and-loss account is coming from fee mix, cost control and acquisitions — not from winning new money.

---

## 6. Concerning and positive signals

**Concerning**

- *April 2025:* The takeover stopped at 89.959%, just under the 90% threshold. That is the worst of both worlds for a minority holder — no buy-out obligation, no delisting, and a permanently thin market. About 10% of the company floats, worth roughly €225 million, trading around €2 million a day.
- *First quarter 2026:* Client assets fell from €212 billion at December to €203.3 billion at March. Even accepting that €5.7 billion of the outflow was the flagged Etica mandate, the direction is down.
- *8 June 2026 onward:* Anima's controlling shareholder is now itself a contested asset in a three-way fight. Every plausible outcome — Intesa Sanpaolo takes Monte dei Paschi, Banco BPM merges with Monte dei Paschi, or nothing happens — changes who controls Anima's distribution.
- *23 June 2026:* The regulator sanctioned the parent for late disclosure on the very capital issue that determines whether it is cheap or expensive for the parent to keep owning Anima.
- *Ongoing:* Goodwill and intangibles are 50.5% of total assets. The apparent cheapness on book-value measures is an accounting artefact.

**Positive**

- *First quarter 2026:* A cost-to-income ratio of 35.5%, with costs falling 1% while net revenue rose 5%. That is real operating leverage, and it is unusual in European asset management.
- *20 April 2026:* A €0.50 ordinary dividend went ex — a trailing yield of 7.2% at today's price, on a payout of about 57%. The cash is being returned, and it has already been paid, so it is not a pending item an investor can still collect on the current price.
- *29 June 2026:* Full control of Castello SGR at a sensible price (€19 million for the last 20%), extending the reach into real assets where fees are higher and stickier than in plain mutual funds.
- *8 July 2026:* June net inflows into managed assets, excluding class-I insurance, were positive at €202 million. Small, but the bleeding after the Etica exit has stopped.
- *Track record:* Six earnings beats in seven quarters, a Piotroski score of 7 out of 9, and free cash flow that comfortably covers the dividend.

---

## 7. Hidden signals

Three quieter observations.

**The "normalised" profit is doing more work than it used to.** In the first quarter of 2026 the gap between reported (€61.4 million) and normalised (€69.9 million) net income was €8.5 million, roughly a seventh of reported profit, and most of it is amortisation of the intangible assets created when Anima bought its distribution mandates. That amortisation reflects a real, running-down asset: the purchased right to manage other people's clients. Treating it as a non-cost is a choice, not a fact.

**The regulator's capital ruling cuts both ways for minority holders.** The European Central Bank refusing the favourable capital treatment makes Anima expensive for Banco BPM to hold. That raises the odds the parent does *something* — either absorbing Anima fully to get the regulatory netting, or selling it. A full sale of control to a third party would, under Italian takeover law, oblige the buyer to offer minorities the same price. That is the single most attractive scenario in this file, and it exists precisely because of a piece of bad news for the parent.

**Nothing in the disclosure discusses the minority.** Across every 2026 release I could source — the first-quarter results, the monthly flows, the Castello completion — there is no reference to the listing, the free float, or the residual stake. The company is being run as a subsidiary that happens to have a quoted stub attached.

---

## 8. Capital-allocation verdict

**Classification: stable.**

Revenue is growing modestly, costs are falling, the return on equity is 14.3%, the dividend is covered, and the acquisitions are small and sensibly priced. This is not a business in trouble and it is not a business accelerating. It is a well-run, low-cost, bank-distributed asset manager whose profit engine is roughly flat and whose growth comes from mix and tuck-ins.

**The single most important thing to weigh before sizing a position:** you are not buying an asset manager, you are buying a 10% remnant of one, and the price of that remnant is set by what a controlling shareholder — itself currently the object of a takeover fight — decides to do next. The operating results will barely matter to the outcome. That is a corporate-event risk with a real probability, not a structural melt.

On today's live multiples Anima trades at 8.8 times trailing earnings, 5.6 times enterprise value to earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation, and yields 7.2%. The discount is a fair price for a permanently illiquid stub with no governance rights, whose distribution depends on banks that are currently being fought over. It is a sound business at a slightly-too-thin discount, not a bargain and not a trap.

# Anima Holding S.p.A. (ANIM.MI) — a deep dive on management and the setup

**Date of review:** 27 July 2026 · **Price used:** €6.94 (Euronext Milan close, 27 July 2026, −1.8% on the day) · **Market value:** about €2.26 billion on roughly 325 million shares

**A note on sources before anything else.** Anima does not publish English-language quarterly earnings-call transcripts, and our data vendor holds none for this listing. There is therefore no multi-quarter transcript series to interrogate, and I will not invent one. What follows is built from what can actually be sourced: the company's own quarterly result releases (most recently the first quarter of 2026, published 4 May 2026), its monthly flow disclosures, the Italian financial press, the Borsa Italiana corporate calendar, and the hard financials in our screener and from the data vendor as of today. Where a management quote appears, it is a translation of the Italian press release as reported by Teleborsa, and it is labelled as such. Where I could not source something, I say so.

---

## 1. Narrative arc

Anima is Italy's largest independent asset manager: it runs mutual funds, institutional mandates and insurance money, with about €203 billion of client assets at the end of March 2026. Almost all of that money reaches Anima through other people's branches — the bank networks of Banco BPM, Monte dei Paschi di Siena, Poste Italiane and Crédit Agricole Italia. That single fact explains both the story management tells and the story the market is actually pricing.

Over the past five years the arc has moved through three phases.

**Phase one (2021–2023) — the fee reset.** Gross commission income fell from €1.23 billion in 2021 to €1.02 billion in both 2022 and 2023, and net income halved from €239 million to €121 million in 2022. This was the bond-market shock working through a book that is unusually heavy in fixed income and insurance-linked products, plus the disappearance of performance fees (the extra fee an asset manager earns only when funds beat a benchmark). Management's language in that period was defensive and cost-focused.

**Phase two (2024–2025) — recovery plus acquisition.** Revenue recovered to €1.32 billion in 2024 and €1.43 billion in 2025, and net income to €228 million and then €266 million. Two things drove it: performance fees came back, and Anima bought its way into new areas — most visibly Castello SGR, a real-estate and alternatives manager, and a broader push beyond plain mutual funds. The narrative shifted from "protect the margin" to "diversify the revenue mix."

**Phase three (from November 2024 to now) — the story stops being about Anima.** On 6 November 2024 Banco BPM launched a takeover for the shares of Anima it did not already own, at €6.20, later raised to €7.00, explicitly aiming to take Anima private. The offer closed in April 2025 with Banco BPM at 89.959% — agonisingly short of the 90% that would have forced a buy-out of the rest and a delisting. Anima has therefore been left as a listed remnant: roughly a tenth of the company still floats, and the other nine-tenths sits with a parent that has said in writing it would rather not have a listing at all.

Since then the operating narrative has become almost secondary. What moves this share is the Italian banking reshuffle: Intesa Sanpaolo's roughly €30.6 billion exchange offer for Monte dei Paschi launched on about 8 June 2026, Monte dei Paschi's board rejecting it as too cheap on 16 July 2026, and the counter-plan for Monte dei Paschi to merge with Banco BPM instead — reported through late July as targeted for early August, with Crédit Agricole (Banco BPM's largest shareholder) publicly cool on it as of 22 July.

---

## 2. Claims versus financials

Management's core claims are that revenue is growing, costs are falling, the mix is diversifying, and the underlying profit is rising even when the headline profit is not. Here is how each holds up.

| Management claim | The evidence | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| Revenue is growing | First-quarter 2026 net revenue €140.6 million, up 5% year on year; net management fees €92.1 million, also up 5% | Holds. Modest, but real and fee-driven rather than one-off |
| Costs are under control | First-quarter 2026 operating costs €39.5 million, down 1%; cost-to-income ratio 35.5% | Holds, and this is genuinely good. A cost-to-income ratio in the mid-thirties is top-quartile for a European asset manager |
| Profit is rising | Reported net income fell 14% to €61.4 million; the "normalised" figure rose 13% to €69.9 million | Holds, but only with the footnote. The 14% fall is explained by €31.8 million of one-off distributor revenue booked in the first quarter of 2025. The comparison base, not the business, moved |
| Client assets are growing | €203.3 billion at March 2026 versus €202.1 billion a year earlier (+1%), but down from €212 billion at December 2025 | Weaker than the story. Net flows in the first quarter were minus €5.8 billion, of which €5.7 billion was the previously-flagged exit of the Etica SGR mandate. Strip that out and flows were roughly flat, not growing |
| Diversification is working | Castello SGR taken to 100% on 29 June 2026, buying Oaktree's remaining 20% for €19 million | Holds directionally, but the scale is small. €19 million for a fifth of Castello implies about €95 million for all of it — roughly 4% of Anima's market value |

Two divergences deserve emphasis.

**The revenue line is not what it looks like.** The €1.47 billion of trailing twelve-month "revenue" in the vendor data is *gross* commission income. Roughly 63% of it is paid straight back out to the banks that distribute the funds. Anima's own reported net revenue runs at about €560 million a year. Anyone anchoring on the €1.47 billion figure — or on a price-to-sales ratio of 1.5 times — is measuring the wrong thing.

**Roughly one fifth of net revenue is performance fees, and those are a market bet.** Performance fees were €29.3 million of the €140.6 million first-quarter net revenue. That slug is genuinely earned, but it appears when markets rise and vanishes when they do not. It disappeared almost entirely in 2022. Any valuation that capitalises it at the same multiple as management fees is overpaying.

Underneath, the returns are respectable and stable: return on equity of 14.3% and return on invested capital of 8.4% on the trailing twelve months, free cash flow of about €250 million against a market value of €2.26 billion (an 11% free-cash-flow yield), and a Piotroski score of 7 out of 9. The gap between those two numbers is the roughly €500 million of investment assets on the books, part of which is seed capital and regulatory capital that is not freely available to shareholders.

One number in the screener's model stack should be discarded outright: a Graham-style margin of safety of +80%. That method leans on book value, and Anima's €5.77 per share of book value is €4.63 per share of goodwill and intangibles — over half of total assets. On tangible book the figure is €1.14 a share. A book-value method applied to an acquisitive asset manager is measuring purchase accounting, not value.

**Stable.** With no call transcripts to trace, the read has to come from the written releases, and those have been consistent rather than escalating. Chief executive Saverio Perissinotto's comment alongside the first-quarter 2026 results (as translated from the Italian release by Teleborsa, 4 May 2026) was that the quarter closed with solid earnings and constructive expectations for the year "despite evident external headwinds," crediting channel diversification and operational efficiency.

That is measured language, and notably it concedes the headwind rather than talking past it. There is no shift into defensive cost-cutting vocabulary — costs are already low and falling — but neither is there the offensive, investment-led language of a company with a growth runway it wants to fund. The tone is that of a mature, well-run utility-like business under an owner that has already decided its future.

## 4. Guidance credibility

**Medium-to-high.** Anima does not give the kind of granular forward guidance that can be scored line by line, but three proxies point the same way. First, the delivery record: our screener shows the company beating consensus in six of the last seven quarters (86%). Second, the Etica SGR mandate loss — €5.7 billion of outflow — was pre-announced rather than sprung on the market, which is the behaviour of a management team that does not manage the news. Third, the reported-versus-normalised gap in the first quarter was clearly bridged to a specific, identifiable prior-year item (€31.8 million of distributor revenue in the base quarter) rather than hidden behind an adjective.

Against that, the consensus now looks for forward earnings per share to *fall* about 2%. Management has not publicly contested that, which suggests either quiet agreement or an absence of the promotional instinct. On this evidence I read it as the latter.

There is one credibility issue in the file, and it belongs to the parent rather than to Anima. On 23 June 2026 Consob, the Italian market regulator, sanctioned Banco BPM for the delay in disclosing that the European Central Bank would not allow the favourable "Danish Compromise" capital treatment to be applied to its Anima acquisition. That is a disclosure failure by the shareholder that controls 90% of this company, on a matter that goes directly to how expensive it is for that shareholder to keep owning Anima. Minority holders should file it.

## 5. Analyst pressure points

Without call transcripts I cannot list questions management deflected. What I can identify are the questions the published materials do not answer, and which any owner of the minority shares needs answered:

- **What happens to the Monte dei Paschi distribution relationship?** Milano Finanza described Monte dei Paschi (11 June 2026) as Anima's principal distributor, and named protecting that alliance as a strategic consideration in how Banco BPM responds to Intesa Sanpaolo. If Intesa Sanpaolo wins Monte dei Paschi, Intesa owns its own large asset manager and has every commercial reason to migrate that money to it over time. Neither Anima nor Banco BPM has publicly quantified what is at stake.
- **What does the parent intend to do with the remaining 10%?** Banco BPM reserved the right to consider future initiatives on the residual stake after April 2025. Fifteen months later there has been no offer, no market buying disclosed to take it past 90%, and no timetable.
- **How much of the €500 million of financial investments is actually surplus?** The company reports a net financial position of €558.3 million but the strict cash-minus-debt figure is €30 million. The bridge is not broken out for outside investors.
- **Where does organic growth come from?** June 2026 managed net inflows, excluding class-I insurance products, were €202 million. On a €203 billion book that is a rounding error. The growth in the profit-and-loss account is coming from fee mix, cost control and acquisitions — not from winning new money.

## 6. Concerning and positive signals

**Concerning**

- *April 2025:* The takeover stopped at 89.959%, just under the 90% threshold. That is the worst of both worlds for a minority holder — no buy-out obligation, no delisting, and a permanently thin market. About 10% of the company floats, worth roughly €225 million, trading around €2 million a day.
- *First quarter 2026:* Client assets fell from €212 billion at December to €203.3 billion at March. Even accepting that €5.7 billion of the outflow was the flagged Etica mandate, the direction is down.
- *8 June 2026 onward:* Anima's controlling shareholder is now itself a contested asset in a three-way fight. Every plausible outcome — Intesa Sanpaolo takes Monte dei Paschi, Banco BPM merges with Monte dei Paschi, or nothing happens — changes who controls Anima's distribution.
- *23 June 2026:* The regulator sanctioned the parent for late disclosure on the very capital issue that determines whether it is cheap or expensive for the parent to keep owning Anima.
- *Ongoing:* Goodwill and intangibles are 50.5% of total assets. The apparent cheapness on book-value measures is an accounting artefact.

**Positive**

- *First quarter 2026:* A cost-to-income ratio of 35.5%, with costs falling 1% while net revenue rose 5%. That is real operating leverage, and it is unusual in European asset management.
- *20 April 2026:* A €0.50 ordinary dividend went ex — a trailing yield of 7.2% at today's price, on a payout of about 57%. The cash is being returned, and it has already been paid, so it is not a pending item an investor can still collect on the current price.
- *29 June 2026:* Full control of Castello SGR at a sensible price (€19 million for the last 20%), extending the reach into real assets where fees are higher and stickier than in plain mutual funds.
- *8 July 2026:* June net inflows into managed assets, excluding class-I insurance, were positive at €202 million. Small, but the bleeding after the Etica exit has stopped.
- *Track record:* Six earnings beats in seven quarters, a Piotroski score of 7 out of 9, and free cash flow that comfortably covers the dividend.

## 7. Hidden signals

Three quieter observations.

**The "normalised" profit is doing more work than it used to.** In the first quarter of 2026 the gap between reported (€61.4 million) and normalised (€69.9 million) net income was €8.5 million, roughly a seventh of reported profit, and most of it is amortisation of the intangible assets created when Anima bought its distribution mandates. That amortisation reflects a real, running-down asset: the purchased right to manage other people's clients. Treating it as a non-cost is a choice, not a fact.

**The regulator's capital ruling cuts both ways for minority holders.** The European Central Bank refusing the favourable capital treatment makes Anima expensive for Banco BPM to hold. That raises the odds the parent does *something* — either absorbing Anima fully to get the regulatory netting, or selling it. A full sale of control to a third party would, under Italian takeover law, oblige the buyer to offer minorities the same price. That is the single most attractive scenario in this file, and it exists precisely because of a piece of bad news for the parent.

**Nothing in the disclosure discusses the minority.** Across every 2026 release I could source — the first-quarter results, the monthly flows, the Castello completion — there is no reference to the listing, the free float, or the residual stake. The company is being run as a subsidiary that happens to have a quoted stub attached.

## 8. Capital-allocation verdict

**Classification: stable.**

Revenue is growing modestly, costs are falling, the return on equity is 14.3%, the dividend is covered, and the acquisitions are small and sensibly priced. This is not a business in trouble and it is not a business accelerating. It is a well-run, low-cost, bank-distributed asset manager whose profit engine is roughly flat and whose growth comes from mix and tuck-ins.

**The single most important thing to weigh before sizing a position:** you are not buying an asset manager, you are buying a 10% remnant of one, and the price of that remnant is set by what a controlling shareholder — itself currently the object of a takeover fight — decides to do next. The operating results will barely matter to the outcome. Size for the fact that roughly €225 million of stock floats, that the parent is under no obligation to buy it, and that the most likely mechanism for a forced buy-out under Italian law (a merger, which grants minorities the right to withdraw at the average price of the prior six months) would pay something close to where the shares already trade, not a premium.

**Economic moat: narrow.** The moat type is contractual distribution — long-dated agreements to run money gathered by Italian bank and post-office branch networks — reinforced by scale-driven cost advantage. The evidence supports "narrow" rather than "wide": returns are solid but not exceptional (return on invested capital 8.4%, return on equity 14.3%), and the pricing power sits with the distributor, not the manager, which is why 63% of gross commissions are paid away. The moat is not eroding on the evidence — margins are stable, the cost ratio is improving, and management fees grew 5% in the latest quarter — but it rests on counterparties Anima does not control.

**Moat trend: stable.** Gross margin is flat, the cost-to-income ratio is improving, and returns are steady to slightly better year on year. Nothing in the numbers points to structural erosion.

**Secular threat: manageable.** The genuine long-run force in this industry is fee compression from index funds and exchange-traded funds. It is real but slow, and Anima is partly insulated: its book is weighted toward insurance-linked and bond products sold through branch networks to savers who do not shop on fee, and its own fees are already low. The far more pressing risk is not secular at all — it is the single-name risk that the Monte dei Paschi distribution relationship ends up inside a rival's group. That is a corporate-event risk with a real probability, not a structural melt.

**Is the cheapness a mispricing or a trap?** Neither, quite. On today's live multiples Anima trades at 8.8 times trailing earnings, 5.6 times enterprise value to earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation, and yields 7.2%. That is cheaper than Amundi (13.6 times) and marginally cheaper than Azimut (9.3 times), but it is not the fire-sale the screener's book-value methods suggest. The discount is a fair price for a permanently illiquid stub with no governance rights, whose distribution depends on banks that are currently being fought over. It is a sound business at a slightly-too-thin discount, not a bargain and not a trap.
